questions.q: A confusion matrix shows TP = 16, FP = 15, FN = 43, TN = 176. What is the recall for the positive class?
questions.explain: Recall is TP / (TP + FN): of the 59 real positives, 16 were found. 0.516 is precision and 0.768 is accuracy.

questions.q: Why can accuracy be misleading for churn prediction?
options: It cannot be computed for binary labels
Most customers stay, so a model that never flags anyone can still score high
questions.explain: With about 76% of customers staying, always predicting 'stayed' gives roughly 76% accuracy while catching no churner. Accuracy hides that failure.

questions.q: Each retention phone call is expensive, so the team wants most flagged customers to really be at risk. Which metric should they emphasize?
questions.explain: Precision measures how many flagged customers are real churners. When false alarms are costly, precision matters most.

questions.q: What does a false negative mean in the churn problem?
options: The model flagged a customer who stayed
The model correctly predicted a customer would stay
The model predicted stay, but the customer churned
questions.explain: A false negative is a miss: a real positive (churner) predicted as negative. It lowers recall.

questions.q: Why did precision_score need zero_division=0 for the always-'stayed' dummy model?
options: The dummy never predicts churn, so TP + FP is zero and precision is undefined
The dummy predicted too many positives
zero_division is required for every metric
questions.explain: Precision = TP / (TP + FP). If a model never predicts the positive class, the denominator is zero and scikit-learn needs to be told what value to report.
